nameStory: This delicate wildflower is named after Thomas Nuttall, a 19th-century English botanist who explored much of North America documenting plants. Nuttall was known for his adventurous spirit and detailed plant collections, making this small but beautiful lobelia a fitting tribute to his botanical legacy.
description: Nuttall's lobelia is a small, delicate perennial wildflower that rarely gets noticed in the wild. It produces tiny pale blue flowers in late summer, standing just a few inches tall among the grasses and sedges of wet, sandy areas. This dainty member of the bellflower family is quite rare in New England, making any sighting a special discovery for nature lovers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale blue flowers bloom in late summer, each with the distinctive lobelia shape - split into upper and lower lips like a snapdragon. The flowers are much smaller and paler than other lobelias you might know.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A small, delicate perennial that stays low to the ground, easily overlooked among taller wetland plants. The whole plant has a fragile, wispy appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow leaves arranged alternately along the stem. They feel thin and delicate to the touch, not thick or waxy like some wetland plants.

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Always found in wet, sandy, acidic soils - think coastal areas, bogs, or pine flatwoods where the ground stays moist but isn't underwater.

habitat: In New England, look for Nuttall's lobelia in coastal wetlands with sandy, acidic soils - places like cranberry bogs, wet pine barrens, or the edges of coastal ponds. It thrives in areas that stay consistently moist but aren't deeply flooded, often growing alongside sedges, sphagnum moss, and other bog plants. This plant needs very specific conditions, which explains why it's so rarely seen in our region.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small rosettes of narrow leaves, easily missed among other emerging wetland vegetation.
seasonality.summer: The plant develops its flowering stems in mid-summer, with the characteristic pale blue blooms appearing in late summer when many other wildflowers are fading.
seasonality.fall: After flowering, the plant produces small seed capsules and begins to die back, becoming increasingly difficult to spot.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground parts, leaving no visible trace above ground during the dormant season.

funFact: With only 2 recorded observations in all of New England, finding Nuttall's lobelia is like discovering botanical treasure - you're more likely to spot a bald eagle than this tiny wildflower!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small blue wetland flowers, but the distinctive lobelia flower shape (split into upper and lower lips) separates it from similar-colored plants like bluets or speedwells, which have regular, symmetrical flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the bellflower family, lobelias have very different flowers from typical bell-shaped campanulas - they're actually quite specialized with their distinctive two-lipped shape that evolved for specific pollinators.
compareHints: Nuttall's lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its famous relatives like cardinal flower (bright red) or great blue lobelia (deep blue and tall). While those species are showy garden favorites, Nuttall's lobelia is a tiny specialist that most people walk right past without noticing. Its pale blue color and diminutive size make it the wallflower of the lobelia family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Cardinal flower stands out dramatically from its lobelia relatives—while great blue lobelia produces similar tubular flowers in blue, and Indian tobacco has tiny pale flowers, only cardinal flower blazes in brilliant red.
Unlike its showier relatives cardinal flower (bright red) and great blue lobelia (deep blue), Indian tobacco has much smaller, paler flowers.
Among New England's lobelias, great blue lobelia is easily distinguished by its brilliant blue color and robust size.
Unlike its showy red cousin cardinal flower or the tall blue spikes of great blue lobelia, water lobelia is the only member of the lobelia family that lives completely underwater.
Among New England's lobelias, pale-spiked lobelia is the wallflower of the family with its subtle white or pale blue flowers.
Kalm's lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its showy relatives like cardinal flower (bright red) or great blue lobelia (deep blue, much larger).
Garden lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its New England native relatives like cardinal flower and great blue lobelia, which are tall, upright wetland plants.

Unlike its native Lobelia relatives such as cardinal flower or great blue lobelia which grow as upright leafy stems with showy flower spikes, matted pratia is a tiny mat-forming groundcover with individual star-shaped flowers.
